st.t: Professional power: AI redistributes tasks and status
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s organisational and sociological framing and materially develops it through a multilevel research agenda linking human–AI interdependence to task redesign, tacit expertise, learning, technologists’ status, business models and governance. It reinforces that outcomes depend on institutional and organisational context rather than technical capability alone, while appropriately treating many consequences as open research questions rather than forecasts.
qs: We argue that an approach is needed focused on emerging and future interdependencies between professionals and GML, something that implies extending but also reimagining theoretical perspectives on expertise, work, and organizations.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core view that GML reconfigures task bundles rather than replacing professionals uniformly, and that outcomes depend on scrutiny, expertise and organisational redesign. It materially extends this proposition with a relational, three-level framework linking professional expertise, individual and group responses, and firm organisation, including the roles of clients and technologists. Its conclusions remain provisional because empirical evidence is sparse.

kp.k: Research agenda, not definitive evidence of generative AI's impacts
kp.d: Faulconbridge and colleagues develop a theoretical research agenda published on 13 March 2026, extending research on digital, algorithmic and extractive machine-learning technologies. They examine expertise at field level, professional responses at individual/group level, and organization at firm level. They acknowledge scarce empirical research on GML and the artificial separation of these interrelated levels; their framework is not a definitive account of impacts on particular professions.
qs: Existing theory provides perti­nent questions, foci, and analytical frames.
greater consideration will be needed of the sys­temic implications of changes that cut across the differ­ent levels.

kp.k: Generative capabilities broaden professional and lay access
kp.d: The authors distinguish GML's generation of new content through recombination from extractive systems' identification of existing information. Natural-language interfaces make adoption easier for professionals and potentially enable other occupations and laypeople to perform professional activities, including generating legal advice. These are proposed mechanisms of change, not measured displacement outcomes.
qs: GML generates new data by remixing and recombining existing content
democratizing ac­cess and use
(e.g. generating legal advice)

kp.d: The central argument treats expertise and agency as relational accomplishments involving professionals, GML, clients, institutions and organizations, rather than properties attributable exclusively to humans or machines. The authors recommend studying how technology design interacts with situated professional practices, capabilities and limitations. This extends existing theory rather than assuming technology alone determines outcomes.
qs: It is, then, the interdependencies between pro­fessionals and GML that need to be the focus of analyses.
agency emerges from the in­terplay within assemblages, which include data, algo­rithms, routines, and decisions

kp.k: Automation estimates do not establish employment losses
kp.d: The paper reports estimates from Eisfeldt et al. (2023) and Singh and O’Keeffe (2023) that about 40% of current professional-services labour time, including law, can be automated. It contrasts suggestions of reduced staffing, particularly among juniors, with Law and Shen's (2025) accounting research indicating possible headcount growth through business expansion. These are attributed estimates and findings, not the authors' own employment measurements or a settled forecast for lawyers.
qs: Some estimate that about 40% of current labour time
due to business growth (Law and Shen 2025)

kp.k: Legal applications span drafting, research and client interactions
kp.d: The paper describes legal uses ranging from document and due-diligence summaries to contracts, filings and court-ruling drafts. Table 1 combines predicted uses and active trials, including client triage and chatbots, legal research, compliance updates, budget forecasting and contract review. Its examples illustrate possible interdependencies rather than establishing adoption prevalence or effectiveness. Human checking for hallucinations remains necessary.

kp.k: Task automation also changes retained professional work
kp.d: Reporting Faulconbridge et al. (2024), the authors explain that extractive machine learning in accounting and law primarily changed diagnosis tasks such as searching, sorting and categorizing data previously handled by juniors. Faster diagnosis also indirectly changed inference and treatment and generated interpretation work. For GML, they propose examining task replacement, preservation and creation together, and questioning whether established task categories and the automation–augmentation distinction remain adequate.

kp.k: Capabilities vary across tasks and collaboration arrangements
kp.d: The authors report Dell’Acqua et al.'s (2023) distinction between fine-grained human–AI integration, or cyborg work, and more separate divisions of labour, or centaur work, across a jagged capability frontier. They also report Mollick's distinction between human-only tasks, delegated tasks whose outputs are checked, and automated tasks whose outputs are not checked. Cited writing-task studies suggest productivity and quality gains may disproportionately benefit less-skilled workers, but the paper cautions that these results do not establish situated professional adoption patterns.

kp.k: Context and relational expertise constrain automation
kp.d: Drawing on Pasquale, Pakarinen and Huising, and Fleming, the paper emphasizes tacit knowledge, client relationships, values and situated judgment as limits to automation. Its discussion of bounded automation distinguishes technical or financial feasibility from politically and organizationally mediated adoption. The research implication is to examine how professionals accommodate both what machines can and cannot know, rather than equating task capability with job replacement.
qs: ‘history, context, configuration, or enactment’
professional jobs are like Gordian Knots
‘bounded auto­mation’

kp.k: Performance benchmarks cannot capture all professional expertise
kp.d: The paper reports Lebovitz et al.'s (2022) argument that narrow machine-performance measures based on ground-truth labels fail to capture professional know-how. It also reports Anthony's (2021) two-year inductive study across four investment banks: partitioning separated junior analysis from senior interpretation, whereas co-construction combined junior interpretation with senior feedback and questioning. The latter supported more considered advice, junior development and identification of technological limitations. These are cross-domain findings used to frame GML research, not new legal-AI benchmark results.

kp.k: AI may support training while weakening experiential learning
kp.d: The authors identify competing mechanisms for professional formation. Digital client twins could let students practise cases and alternative outcomes, while different modes of human–AI collaboration could generate new learning opportunities. Conversely, they report research suggesting opaque systems and uncritical reliance on algorithmic decisions can dilute experiential learning and weaken expertise, especially among juniors. They call for research on how apprenticeship can preserve scrutiny, reflection and mastery.
qs: GML can enable the development of a digital client ‘twin’

kp.k: Identity, interests and ethical risks shape adoption
kp.d: The paper organizes professional responses around resistance, identity, jurisdictional boundaries and collaboration. It argues that professional status, meaningful work, political interests and sensemaking affect adoption alongside technical capabilities. Privacy, bias, hallucinations, opacity and accountability may prompt hesitation, while controlled use may preserve valued identities or help form new ones. Professionals and regulators must address supervision and responsibility, but the paper does not prescribe particular legal professional rules.
qs: professionals will make and give sense to GML
‘who we are’ and ‘what we do’

kp.k: Jurisdictions and technologist roles may be reconfigured
kp.d: The authors suggest that client self-service and nonprofessionals using GML could circumvent established jurisdictions, while professionals might defend existing boundaries or expand into new services. They report earlier research showing technologists becoming involved in producing and delivering legal advice rather than remaining support staff. New brokers and hybrid roles may enable collaboration but also create boundaries, dependencies and shifts in hierarchy, status and power.

‘technologists’, ‘translators’, or ‘algorithmic brokers’

kp.k: Business models, staffing and hourly pricing face questions
kp.d: Building on Armour and Sako (2020), the authors identify scalability, routinization and process efficiency as possible bases for new business models. They ask how GML will change workforce size and composition, staffing leverage, capital intensity, costs, pricing and client offerings. Whether hourly billing survives, firms hire hybrid professionals or parallel specialist teams, and change occurs within incumbents or new AI-ready firms remains an open research agenda rather than an established market outcome.
qs: new business models oriented around scalability, rou­tinization, and process efficiency
will the billable hour survive in legal work?

kp.k: Governance may evolve through hybrid organizational forms
kp.d: The paper argues that greater technological investment and distributed expertise could challenge professional autonomy, partnership governance and the traditional low-capital-intensity basis of PSFs. It considers corporate hierarchies and digital networks but regards evolutionary, layered and hybrid responses as plausible based on earlier research. Outcomes may differ between regulated and newer professions, traditional partnerships and alternative business structures, and firms with different funding arrangements; complementary human skills remain important.

kp.k: Innovation requires balancing central control and local experimentation
kp.d: Drawing on Goto (2023) and Dodgson et al. (2022), the authors discuss more formal, anticipatory innovation structures alongside leadership and experimental spaces. They identify tensions between top-down standardization and bottom-up experimentation, mediated by regulation, professional knowledge cultures and risk tolerance. These choices affect governance and the range of organizational forms that may emerge.

kp.k: Client relations mediate augmentation versus direct substitution
kp.d: The authors contrast professionals adapting AI-generated material before delivery with clients consuming chatbot outputs directly, while allowing hybrid arrangements. GML could support both efficiency and differentiated relational service, potentially freeing professionals for bespoke interpersonal work. They also report research warning that perceived harms can deter clients from using services. The balance between useful delegation and inappropriate substitution is therefore contingent on client feedback, professional norms and organizational learning, not simply technical capability.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Faulconbridge and co-authors anticipate a reconfiguration of professional work through human–GML interdependencies, rather than a uniform replacement of professionals.
pts.d: The authors argue that generative machine learning (GML) extends AI beyond extracting information into generating material used in diagnosis, inference and advice. Their legal examples include document summaries, due-diligence reports, contract drafting and review, client triage, research and client-facing chatbots. They expect combinations of task replacement, preservation, augmentation and the creation of new tasks. Human expertise remains important for contextual interpretation, client relationships and checking hallucinations. They identify possible improvements in junior professionals’ productivity alongside risks to apprenticeship and expertise development when outputs are accepted without scrutiny. They also anticipate changes in professional identity, jurisdictional boundaries and collaboration with technologists. At firm level, they expect disruption to business models, work allocation, investment, governance and client service, with greater diversity among professional service firms (PSFs). Increased capital intensity and reduced dependence on credentialed professionals are conditional possibilities, not established outcomes. The survival of hourly billing, the direction of headcount change and the emergence of new firm forms are explicitly unresolved questions, not firm predictions.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: This is principally a literature-based research agenda, supplemented by illustrative applications, rather than a new empirical test of GML’s effects on legal services.
pts.d: The authors extrapolate from research on digital technologies, algorithms, extractive machine learning and emerging GML. Their account of changes to legal and accounting tasks draws on Faulconbridge et al. (2024), which studied extractive machine learning rather than GML. Their discussion of productivity and reduced performance disparities cites Dell’Acqua et al. (2023) and Noy and Zhang (2023); these knowledge-work writing studies do not establish equivalent effects across situated legal practice. The approximately 40% automation estimate is presented as an external estimate attributed to Eisfeldt et al. (2023) and Singh and O’Keeffe (2023), not the authors’ own measurement or a forecast of equivalent job losses. Contrasting headcount possibilities draw on Sampson (2021) and Law and Shen (2025), the latter concerning audit firms. Learning risks draw on studies including Anthony’s investment-bank research and Sundaresan and Guler’s clinical-care research. Business-model and governance possibilities build on Armour and Sako, Kronblad and other PSF scholarship. Table 1 is labelled as based on the authors’ field research but combines predicted or trialled uses and citations to case studies, professional bodies and commercial publications; it does not provide a controlled assessment of those applications. The cited court-citation incident illustrates hallucination risk rather than measuring a model error rate. The authors acknowledge limited empirical GML research and do not supply their own quantitative legal productivity, employment or market-impact results.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The article addresses emergent adoption and an unspecified future; outcomes depend on technological capabilities, professional responses and organizational conditions.
pts.d: Published in March 2026, the article describes experimentation and applications predicted or being trialled at the time of writing. It reports short-to-medium-term disruption expectations but provides no dated timetable for workforce restructuring, pricing changes or replacement of firm forms. The authors qualify productivity possibilities by current tool capabilities and the uneven, changing frontier between human and machine performance. Adoption and effects depend on professional knowledge, identity, ethics, trust, regulation, organizational governance, funding, risk tolerance and client preferences. Automation potential is therefore not equivalent to realized automation. Human checking is required where hallucinations threaten reliability, and learning outcomes depend on whether professionals scrutinize, reflect on and question outputs. Increased capital intensity is conditional on greater codification and a larger GML role in producing professional outputs. The authors leave open whether established firms adapt or new firms emerge and emphasize that different professions and firm types may follow different paths.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The anticipated changes concern lawyers and other professionals, juniors and trainees, technologists, clients, and differently organized professional service firms.
pts.d: Lawyers may increasingly work from machine-generated drafts and analyses while contributing contextual judgment, client understanding and verification. Juniors and apprentices may gain productivity but lose opportunities to learn through foundational tasks; the authors do not conclude that junior employment must fall. Experienced professionals may need to revise their identities and work practices, with resistance or controlled adoption shaping outcomes. Technologists, translators and algorithmic brokers may become more central to producing advice, potentially changing authority and status within firms. Paraprofessionals, other occupations and lay users may gain access to activities previously associated with professional expertise, creating possible competition and jurisdictional change. Clients may receive faster or differently configured services through self-service, chatbots and human–AI combinations, but concerns about errors, data security and harmful consequences can discourage use. PSFs face potential changes to staffing, costs, pricing, capital requirements and governance. Effects may differ between regulated traditional professions and newer professional services, between partnerships and alternative business structures, and between differently funded firms. Accounting, medicine, finance and other professions supply cross-domain examples; their findings are not presented as direct measurements of legal-market outcomes. The matrimonial-service examples illustrate possible access-to-justice applications, not measured closure of the justice gap.
